blocks.label: greedy feasibility checker
blocks.py:
def feasible(cap):                      # can we split into <= k parts?
    students, cur = 1, 0
    for p in pages:
        if p > cap: return False
        if cur + p > cap: students += 1; cur = p
        else: cur += p
    return students <= k
# bisect: lo=max(pages), hi=sum(pages); find FIRST true

sections.title: Partition bisection — median of two sorted arrays

blocks.md: The MAANG boss fight. Median splits merged order at half-point; find a CUT i in shorter array such that left-parts contain exactly ⌈(m+n)/2⌉ elements AND every left value ≤ every right value across BOTH arrays. Binary search the cut.

blocks.label: partition search core
blocks.py:
# A shorter; search cut i in [0,m]; j = half - i
while lo <= hi:
    i = (lo + hi) // 2; j = half - i
    Al = A[i-1] if i else float("-inf"); Ar = A[i] if i < m else float("inf")
    Bl = B[j-1] if j else float("-inf"); Br = B[j] if j < n else float("inf")
    if Al <= Br and Bl <= Ar:
        return max(Al, Bl) if (m+n) % 2 else (max(Al,Bl)+min(Ar,Br)) / 2
    if Al > Br: hi = i - 1      # too many big-A on left -> pull left
    else:       lo = i + 1

sections.title: Problem set — L3 hard (your .cpp files weaponized)

items.title: Allocate Minimum Number of Pages
items.statement: Re-solve with full monotonicity narration + trace table like section example.

solutionCode.label: minimise the maximum load; feasibility is monotone increasing

items.complexity: O(n · log(sum − max)) — a linear greedy check inside a binary search over the page range. Space O(1).

followups.a: studentsNeeded(cap) is non-increasing in cap: raising the page limit can only let a student absorb more books, never fewer. So "cap is feasible" (needs ≤ m students) is false for small caps and true from some point on — the FFFF TTTT shape. You hunt the first true.

followups.q: Why is lo = max(books) rather than 0?
followups.a: A cap below the largest single book is infeasible at any student count — that book fits nowhere. Starting the range there is not just an optimisation: with lo = 0 the greedy checker would loop forever or need an extra guard, since no assignment exists.

items.title: Aggressive Cows
items.statement: Largest minimum distance. Sort stalls; bisect distance.

solutionCode.label: maximise the minimum gap; hunt the LAST feasible distance

items.complexity: O(n log n) to sort, then O(n · log(maxDist)) for the search. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why does this hunt the LAST true while B301 hunts the FIRST?
followups.a: The predicates point opposite ways. "Cap is feasible" becomes true as cap grows, so the minimum feasible cap is the first true. "Distance d is achievable" becomes false as d grows, so the maximum achievable d is the last true. Same skeleton, mirrored branch — identifying which shape you have is the whole decision.

followups.q: Why is the greedy checker optimal?
followups.a: Placing the first cow at the leftmost stall is never worse: any valid arrangement can be shifted left without reducing the count. From there, taking the earliest stall that satisfies the gap leaves the most room for the remaining cows. An exchange argument makes greedy exact, which is what licenses using it as the feasibility oracle.

items.title: Painter's Partition Problem
items.statement: Same skeleton as B301 — prove equivalence sentence instead of re-deriving.

solutionCode.label: the same problem with different nouns

items.complexity: Identical to B301: O(n · log(sum)). Space O(1).

followups.a: "Both split a fixed-order sequence into k contiguous groups minimising the maximum group sum." Boards are books, painters are students, and the per-unit paint time is a constant multiplier that does not change which partition is optimal. Nothing needs re-deriving.

followups.q: Why does the fixed order matter?
followups.a: Both problems forbid reordering — a student gets consecutive books, a painter gets adjacent boards. That is what makes the greedy checker valid. If reordering were allowed it becomes bin-packing, which is NP-hard, and binary search on the answer no longer has a polynomial oracle.

items.title: Koko Eating Bananas
items.statement: Min eating speed finishing within h hours.

solutionCode.label: hours(speed) is non-increasing; hunt the first feasible speed

followups.q: Why is the upper bound max(piles) rather than sum(piles)?
followups.a: Koko eats at most one pile per hour regardless of speed — a speed above the largest pile finishes every pile in exactly one hour and cannot go faster. So max(piles) already achieves the minimum possible hour count; anything larger is wasted range.

It is integer ceiling division without floating point. Using p/speed truncates and undercounts the final partial hour; using ceil(double) invites rounding error at large values. The idiom is exact and stays in integers — it reappears in B404 verbatim.

items.title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
items.statement: Least ship weight capacity; order fixed.

solutionCode.label: days(capacity) is non-increasing; order is fixed

followups.q: How is this different from Allocate Minimum Pages?
followups.a: It is not — same shape, same checker, same bounds. Packages are books, days are students, capacity is the page cap. Recognising the third instance of one pattern in a row is the actual skill this trio is drilling.

followups.q: What does "order is fixed" rule out?
followups.a: Sorting the packages. If you could reorder, you would pack greedily by weight and get a smaller capacity — but the conveyor delivers in a fixed sequence, so groups must be contiguous. Sorting here silently solves a different, easier problem.

items.title: SPOJ EKO — Wood Cutting
items.statement: Max saw height collecting ≥ M wood. Verdict flips direction vs B301.

solutionCode.label: wood(H) is non-increasing; hunt the LAST feasible height

followups.q: Which direction does the verdict flip, versus B301?
followups.a: B301's feasibility improves as the cap *rises*, so you hunt the first true and shrink hi. Here feasibility degrades as the height rises — more height means less wood — so you hunt the last true and grow lo. Getting this backwards is the single most common bug in answer-space search; state the direction before writing the branch.

followups.q: Why is lo = 0 valid here when B301 needed lo = max?
followups.a: Height 0 is always feasible — it harvests every tree entirely. There is no infeasible floor to exclude, unlike a page cap below the largest book. The bounds come from the problem's semantics, not from a template.

items.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
hints: Parity branch + sentinels; hand-trace {1,2},{3,4} before coding.

solutionCode.label: binary search the CUT position, with infinite sentinels
solutionCode.py:
def find_median_sorted_arrays(A: list[int], B: list[int]) -> float:
    if len(A) > len(B):
        A, B = B, A                       # search the shorter array
    m, n = len(A), len(B)
    lo, hi = 0, m                         # cut position in A: 0..m
    INF = float('inf')
    while lo <= hi:
        i = lo + (hi - lo) // 2           # take i from A
        j = (m + n + 1) // 2 - i          # ...so the total left half is fixed
        # sentinels remove every empty-side special case
        a_left = -INF if i == 0 else A[i - 1]
        a_right = INF if i == m else A[i]
        b_left = -INF if j == 0 else B[j - 1]
        b_right = INF if j == n else B[j]

        if a_left <= b_right and b_left <= a_right:        # correct cut
            if (m + n) % 2:
                return float(max(a_left, b_left))          # odd: left max
            return (max(a_left, b_left) + min(a_right, b_right)) / 2.0
        if a_left > b_right:
            hi = i - 1                    # took too many from A
        else:
            lo = i + 1                    # took too few
    return 0.0

items.complexity: O(log(min(m, n))) — the search runs over the shorter array only. Space O(1).

followups.a: m=2, n=2, half=(4+1)/2=2. First i=1, j=1: Aleft=1, Aright=2, Bleft=3, Bright=4. Aleft(1) ≤ Bright(4) but Bleft(3) > Aright(2), so we took too few from A — lo=2. Next i=2, j=0: Aleft=2, Aright=+∞, Bleft=−∞, Bright=3. Both conditions hold. Even total, so (max(2,−∞) + min(+∞,3))/2 = (2+3)/2 = 2.5.

followups.q: What do the sentinels actually buy?
followups.a: They turn four boundary cases — cut at the very start or end of either array — into ordinary arithmetic. Without them you need explicit i==0 / i==m / j==0 / j==n branches inside the comparison, which is where nearly every failed attempt at this problem breaks. −∞ never violates a ≤ on the left; +∞ never violates one on the right.
